#7543. YouTube enlists educational creators to show the value of its interactive gaming hub

As educators, researchers, and policymakers debate YouTube’s utility in classrooms, a handful of creators are getting the chance to show how the platform’s interactive elements can enhance learning. YouTube quietly introduced a slate of educational games through its Playables hub, with notable STEM channels like Veritasium and Khan Academy involved in the initiative.

Playables has been available on YouTube for nearly three years, but for much of its existence, the hub has been little more than a motley collection of low-stakes, casual titles. Though YouTube has tested some upgrades for its gaming destination, the reach and influence of Playables pale in comparison to YouTube’s traditional video library.

Last week, YouTube showed that Playables could have significant potential in scholastic settings. With its six-game library of educational titles, YouTube is helping players learn about subjects like physics, economics, and music theory within fun, interactive settings.

Daily industry updates, straight to your inbox.

Veritasium’s contribution to the new gaming library is Elements of Truth, a simple trivia challenge that tests players’ scientific knowledge. According to Luke Lewis, the Director of Publishing at Electrify Video Partners — which invested in Veritasium in 2023 — YouTube came calling earlier this year to propose Playables tie-ins for Electrify’s brands. Lewis told Tubefilter that Electrify saw the proposal as an opportunity to promote Veritasium’s Elements of Truth tabletop game.

“Our long-term expectations are for the game to introduce Elements of Truth to an audience of knowledge-hungry casual gamers who might otherwise not be familiar with it – and in fact might not even be familiar with Veritasium‘s videos,” Lewis said. “At the same time, we hope it will deepen engagement among existing Veritasium fans, encourage them to get competitive with fellow fans, and have fun doing it.”

Lewis said that the initial response to the Playables title has been “extremely positive.” Orders for the physical Elements of Truth game have spiked as Veritasium fans have shared their Playables high scores with each other.

As useful as Playables has been for Electrify and Veritasium, it might be even more valuable for YouTube itself. Though the platform has thrown resources behind educational initiatives led by top creators, it has also faced ban threats in schools, most notably in the New York City school district. Detractors may argue that a platform like YouTube can only be a distraction in the classroom, but games like Elements of Truth suggest otherwise.

In previous years, interactive games on YouTube have been the domain of marketing agencies and tech-savvy tinkerers. Perhaps, given the positive response Electrify has seen, we’re about to enter into an era of good-for-you games on Google’s video platform. YouTube is certainly committed to promoting Playables. It recently introduced accessability tags that help users find the games that best fit their device’s settings. So if you want to try to beat my Elements of Truth high score (which won’t be too hard), finding and playing the game should be a cinch.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

A shared robots.txt line could let sites opt out of AI training with several providers at once, but companies involved are handling it differently.

Google, Microsoft, and OpenAI announced plans on Friday to honor a shared robots.txt line for AI training preferences. A site could use it to state one training preference to every provider that takes part, instead of writing rules for each company’s crawler.

The line is from an Internet Draft that Anthropic’s Kevin Kelley submitted to the AI Preferences working group at the IETF (same date). This is listed in the IETF’s document tracker as an individual draft, which does not represent official IETF standardization activity. In a post to the working group’s email list, Kelley indicated that Anthropic has started development to provide this feature.

Based on their provided timelines, none of the three companies currently supports the line. Google and Microsoft described how each would handle it differently. According to Google, if a site sets up a shared opt-out line, Google plans to treat it like a Google-Extended block when a website doesn’t specify Google-Extended, and this control also applies to grounding within Gemini Apps. Microsoft wants sites that use its NoArchive and NoCache tags to switch to new preferences by March 1, 2027.

Kelley’s draft adds no new directive to robots.txt. An ordinary rule group, that a site might write under what the draft calls a policy token, __usage_ai-training, would be written like it always has been, using Allow and Disallow. The draft provides an example of how one might opt out of AI training on the entire site, except for the /press-kit/ folder.

The token itself has its meaning based upon the working group’s vocabulary draft, specifically defining AI Training as using content to modify a generative AI model’s learned parameters. Those models that do nothing but non-generative tasks like classification or ranking are exempted from this definition.

Rules that have already been put into robots.txt files will not be considered as part of any shared training preference. In the draft, a wildcard group (User-Agent: *) can never match the token, and a file without a __usage_ai-training group indicates no preference, which Kelley states is true of every robots.txt file currently published. The token doesn’t control crawling either.

On Oct. 22, I covered a different working group draft, co-written by Google’s Gary Illyes, that would add a Content-Usage rule to robots.txt. Kelley wrote that the group set that draft aside to make progress on the vocabulary.

Google’s post, by John Mueller, says that when a site opts out of training with the shared line and doesn’t specify Google-Extended, Google plans to interpret that “as if the publisher had disallowed Google-Extended.” Google aims to support the control in 2027, according to the post, and its crawler documentation says early 2027.

The documentation says Google-Extended controls whether content can be used to train future Gemini models and whether it can be used for grounding in Gemini Apps and on Vertex AI. Grounding, in Google’s description, means supplying content from the search index to the model when it answers. The post adds that sites that specifically allow Google-Extended are eligible to appear in Gemini Apps responses through grounding.

The documentation also says Google-Extended doesn’t affect a site’s inclusion in Google Search. AI Overviews and AI Mode have a separate opt-out, the Search generative AI control in Search Console, which I covered when it rolled out worldwide in August.

Microsoft’s post, by Bing principal product manager Krishna Madhavan, adopts the shared line for training and adds a separate AI Grounding preference. That one is set only at the page level and governs whether content can help inform AI-generated answers. Microsoft also lets a meta tag or HTTP header set the training preference for a single page, overriding robots.txt for that page.

A default of Allow is what happens with grounding, and keeping a page out is how Disallow works. The new option called DisallowExtended allows grounding in Microsoft created tools like Copilot and Bing’s AI Mode but does not allow grounding through Microsoft provided grounding services that are used by other businesses (Web IQ). Microsoft said either restriction will limit visibility of your brand in answers using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and will have no effect on your ability to be listed in search results from Bing.

Microsoft is replacing NoArchive and NoCache for training and grounding with these two new options. They will begin honoring the new options on February 1, 2027, as they crawl, and they will stop recognizing the older tags as training or grounding options after March 1, 2027.

Sites that use the old tags and want to stay out of grounding also need to record a temporary preference in Bing Webmaster Tools. The setting opens Dec. 15 and is available only to sites still using those tags on that date. Microsoft’s FAQ says pages without one by March 1 default to allowing grounding until Microsoft recrawls them. Microsoft also says that once it detects either new preference on a site, it will disregard any NoArchive or NoCache tags still on that site.

OpenAI aims to honor the signal in the next few months, though its current robots.txt policy will still be in effect.

Neither OpenAI’s blog post nor its crawler documentation (checked Oct. 30) states what would happen when a website has both a shared line rule and GPTBot rule that conflict with each other.

As of Oct. 30, there was no posting in Anthropic’s newsroom regarding the signal. According to Kelley’s mailing list message, implementing support for this feature across all of Anthropic’s services will take some time.

According to Anthropic’s crawler-help webpage (checked Oct. 30), they have only three crawl control options available, which are ClaudeBot, Claude-User, and Claude-SearchBot.

One robots.txt group could replace a stack of per-company training rules once each company reads it; however, an opt-out through the shared line won’t reach the same uses at Google and Microsoft. For example, at Microsoft, training and grounding are separate settings. In contrast, both sit under Google-Extended at Google, and there is no way described in the crawler documentation to keep content out of Gemini training while still letting Gemini Apps use it for grounding.

Microsoft’s is the only announcement that replaces controls sites already use. According to Google, OpenAI, and Anthropic’s Kelley, existing controls will continue to work, so sites that use NoArchive or NoCache to limit how Copilot uses their content have things they need to do first.

OpenAI’s post encourages other AI providers to honor the signal, and Kelley wrote that he hopes others will join. Google and OpenAI say they’ll share more details as their support arrives. Kelley’s draft expires May 3, 2027, unless a new version replaces it, and he plans to propose his design as a change to the Content-Usage draft.

Follow on YouTube. Matt G. Southern is the Senior News Writer at Search Engine Journal, where he’s covered Google, SEO, ...

#7541. FinOps Data Engineer at Supabase

About the RoleWe're looking for a FinOps Data Engineer to help drive cost optimization and cloud financial governance across our AWS infrastructure and GCP footprint. You'll work cross-functionally with Engineering, Finance, and Product to find and ship savings, build the tooling necessary to maximize efficiency of every dollar spent in the cloud, and cultivate a culture of cost awareness across engineering teams. This role owns the data side of that mission: the models, pipelines, and analysis that make cost, usage, and margin numbers trustworthy across the company.This is a hands-on engineering role, not an analyst seat. You'll do the schlep work other teams don't have time for, digging into a bucket's access pattern, writing the dbt model or Python pipeline that ships the fix, building the cost-vs-revenue mart that answers a margin question once instead of every time, and chasing a number until it reconciles. Strong communication matters as much as technical depth, you'll regularly explain a savings case or a data model's implications to an engineering team, a finance stakeholder, and a leadership audience in the same week.What You'll Be Responsible ForIn this role, you'll:

Find and ship savings across AWS and GCP: Analyze billing, usage, and cost trends to identify opportunities, rightsizing, storage lifecycle policies, data transfer, and spot/auto-scaling. Take ideas from identification through to a realized dollar figure, not just a recommendation.

Build and maintain the FinOps data pipeline: Design and run the BigQuery/dbt models that turn raw billing and usage data (CUR, Storage Lens) into reconciled, trustworthy mart tables, the foundation everything else in FinOps is built on.

Build cost-vs-revenue and customer segmentation models: Model unit economics and margin by product line and customer segment, and extend coverage as new products and segments come online.

Apply data science to cost and usage data: Build forecasting models, detect anomalies statistically rather than by threshold alone, and quantify savings opportunities (e.g. storage lifecycle, request-cost patterns) with rigor a spreadsheet can't match.

Build and maintain cost attribution: Tagging policies, cost allocation, and chargeback/showback so engineering teams can see and own their own spend. This is foundational work other savings work depends on.

Automate cost governance: Build automated cost reporting, anomaly detection, and alerting. Write the scripts and infrastructure-as-code (Python, Terraform, Lambda) that enforce cost policy rather than relying on manual review.

Partner with engineering on architecture decisions: Bring cost into the room early, cost-efficiencies are cheaper to get right at design than to retrofit.

Work with Finance on forecasting and reporting: Support budget tracking and financial KPIs; build dashboards and self-serve analytics engineering and finance can both read.

Have strong AWS expertise and working GCP knowledge, including pricing models, billing structures, and cost optimization mechanics.

Have data engineering depth: dbt, BigQuery (or an equivalent modern warehouse), SQL at scale, and data modeling for analytics (dimensional modeling, incremental models, testing).

Have data science fundamentals: statistical forecasting, anomaly detection, and experimentation, and know when a rigorous model beats a rule of thumb.

Have automation and scripting skills: Python, Terraform/ pulumi, Lambda, or Bash.

Are comfortable with cost/billing tooling: AWS Cost Explorer, Cost & Usage Reports, GCP Billing Reports, and BI/dashboarding (we use Hex).

Have experience with, or are comfortable picking up, Linear and Notion as the system of record for tracking and documenting FinOps work.

Experience with a dedicated cloud cost management platform (e.g. CloudZero, Vantage, or similar) is a plus, not required.

Can analyze cost data and present it clearly to both technical and non-technical audiences.

Have prior experience spanning data analytics, data engineering, or data science in a FinOps, cloud cost management, or cloud governance context.

Are energized by doing the unglamorous, high-leverage work (the schlep) that unblocks other teams, and by working cross-functionally without positional authority.

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

Google's John Mueller cast doubt on short-term AI SEO tactics and explained that traditional technical SEO remains relevant.

In a recent interview conducted by David Iwanow, Google’s John Mueller discussed the future of SEO in AI Search, explaining which traditional practices will continue to matter and that the rise of AI Search doesn’t necessarily change what makes a successful SEO strategy.

The interviewer asked John Mueller about listicles. Listicles are like lists of “top companies” that have been used by companies as a way to influence AI chatbots to rank the company creating the listicle as the top choice in their industry. The interviewer acknowledged their usefulness in general but also pointed out that they’ve also been abused and turned into slop content.

Mueller responded that building a solid foundation for a website is preferable to relying on short-term tactics because those always have an expiration date, whereas a site that focuses on quality, what Mueller terms a solid foundation, doesn’t face that kind of expiration date where traffic disappears.

“I think, when I take a step back, like this happens all the time, right? It’s like something comes out and people realize, oh, this actually works particularly well. And then everyone goes off and does it and half the people go off and do it in a particularly bad way.

And then at some point the systems catch up and they’re like, oh, anything that has a listicle is a sign that it’s spam. And it’s like the circle closes and you find something else.

From that point of view, I wouldn’t necessarily say anything that is a listicle is spam.

…It needs to add value. And I think it’s really important to keep in mind that all of these systems are very new, meaning they’re still very much evolving very quickly.

So if you go all out and say, my whole strategy is listicles, then at some point that’s going to switch off and you’re left with nothing really.

Building up a serious, stable foundation for a website, I think that’s the most critical part. And if there are ways that you can play around with some things along the way?

Try things out, maybe that’s fine. But I think you really need to focus on that end goal of having something that search engines and AI systems will want to show to people in the long run.”

The interviewer lamented that shady SEO companies are utilizing low-quality AI SEO tactics in order to rank their clients.

Mueller said that SEOs using shady tactics is not anything new, saying that they did that for regular SEO and now some are doing it for AI SEO.

Mueller recommended that businesses keep a close eye on what outside SEOs are doing, advising that businesses should never just take an SEO company’s word about what they’re doing. That’s good advice because I know there are shady SEO companies who charge a monthly retainer and essentially do nothing but generate a monthly ranking report (at best), while others will engage in low-quality tactics like buying links and so on (at worst).

“But that’s always been the case, right? It’s like you’re paying consultants and they do, I don’t know, keyword stuffing. Or back in the early days, it’s like white text on white background.

And it’s like, it works for a bit, but at some point, it doesn’t work. So I think as a small business, you have to always question what your vendors are doing and always think about..”

Mueller explained that AI system answers rely on factors that are inherently classic SEO, and for that reason, he expects technical SEO will continue to be important. Although AI systems may crawl websites differently depending on their objectives, he sees those differences as extensions of familiar technical SEO and not as evidence that traditional SEO is becoming obsolete.

The context of Mueller’s answer was the interviewer mentioning that Mueller has said in the past that there’s no reason to create special markdown pages for (Google’s) AI Search and asking him if AEO/GEO is dead.

“I think you’ll see that a lot of the AI systems, they build on SEO. So from that point of view, I think it’s going to continue to be relevant. I think especially technical SEO is going to remain very relevant.

It’ll be a little bit different because my understanding is AI systems crawl slightly differently. They have different intents with regards to crawling because they want to do it for training versus just like getting the freshest content. But that’s just is like another flavor of technical SEO. So I think that’s great.”

Something that many experienced SEOs see (and I have over 25 years’ experience) is that people who are relatively new to SEO are rediscovering old ways of doing things, and so there is a resurgence in old, old tactics like cloaking (showing one thing to AI crawlers and something else to users) as if that’s something new. And even the listicle is an old tactic, and I’m even seeing people who are promoting the use of directories and reciprocal links, both of which are super old-school tactics.

Meanwhile, the actual SEO that gets overlooked, things like presenting a strong user experience and promoting content to relevant demographics, married to proven strategies like promoting a website so as to build a positive awareness of a website, those things continue to be as relevant today as they have been throughout the history of SEO.

I have 25 years hands-on experience in SEO, evolving along with the search engines by keeping up with the latest ...

#7536. 3 AI Models Shopped Shopify’s Catalog – Each Picked A Different Winner via @sejournal, @slobodanmanic

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Three Claude models picked from the same 20 Shopify products 1,980 times and never agreed on the top product. Here is what decided their picks.

I gave three AI models the same 20 products and the same request in six searches. They never agreed on which one to buy. When a shopper asks an AI agent for nothing more than the product, the choice between the products on offer comes from the model’s preference, and I tested exactly that, on purpose: no budget, no taste, no shopper history, only the search words. For coffee, I searched Shopify’s catalog for “coffee beans” once, through Shop MCP, the connection Shopify opened to AI agents on Oct. 13, and saved the top 20 results. Then I gave three Claude models that same saved list, the same instruction, and the same request, 50 times each. Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5 favored the dark roast with the most reviews. Opus 5 picked the medium roast 48 times out of 50, and told me why: “With no stated preferences, a medium roast is the safest crowd-pleaser…”

On Oct. 13, 2026, Shopify announced Shop MCP, which, in Shopify’s words, “lets your agent or app search Shopify Catalog, build carts, and complete Shop Pay checkout through a single MCP connection.” It covers over a billion products, and searching needs no API key. Any company building a shopping agent can now search Shopify’s catalog without an API key and get back a list of products for a shopper’s request. It is one of several routes into agentic commerce, the agents that find, compare, and buy for a shopper.

A list is not a purchase. Something has to pick one product off it, and when an agent runs on a language model, the model is what picks. The agent hands the model the products and the request and asks it to choose. The company that builds the agent writes its instructions on top, and those matter. They are also private, and they differ from one agent to the next.

So I tested the part underneath, the model by itself. Same products, same short instruction, same request, and the only thing that changed was the model. If three models given exactly the same input pick different products, then which store gets a customer’s order depends partly on which model the customer’s agent happens to run on.

I have covered the step before this one. In October, I found that Shopify’s catalog ranks products with more reviews higher. This test starts where that one stopped: once the catalog has returned its list, what does the model choose from it?

I ran each search once through Shop MCP, as an anonymous U.S. buyer, and saved the top 20 results. Every call to a model got that same saved list, in the catalog’s order (except in the test where I reversed it), so the products never changed between models or between runs. Eight skincare searches were fetched on 15 October. Six more, backpack, coffee beans, running shoes, water bottle, wireless earbuds and yoga mat, were fetched on Oct. 24. I also fetched “scented candle” and “dog food” and dropped them, because one store filled all 20 candle results and three stores filled the dog food list.

For each product the model saw the title, the store, the price, the star rating and review count, the catalog’s one-line summary and its first three listed features, numbered 1 to 20. It saw nothing else. The instruction, word for word:

You are a shopping agent. A person has asked you to buy something for them. You will see the products the Shopify catalog returned for their request. Choose the one product you would buy for them. Reply with JSON only, no other text: {“pick”: , “reason”: “”}

Then came the shopper’s request, which was only the search words: “coffee beans”, “water bottle”, “mineral sunscreen SPF 50”. In one test I added a budget and a skin type.

The models were Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5, run through Claude Code with default settings, no tools and no web access. Every pick was a fresh call with no memory of the others.

There were three sets of runs, 1,980 picks in all:

The reason for the bare setup is the point of the test. No preferences, no shopping history, no system prompt from an agent company. This is the raw response from the model when it has no other inputs, and how it differs depending on the model. Every real agent adds more on top, so this is the layer everything else gets built on.

On the six product searches, the three models’ most-picked product matched in none. Haiku and Sonnet agreed on three (backpack, coffee beans, water bottle), Sonnet and Opus on two (wireless earbuds, yoga mat), and Haiku and Opus on one (running shoes).

Each model was consistent with itself, and the models were not consistent with each other. Sonnet’s most-picked product took 94% of its picks on average across the six searches, Opus’s took 89%, and Haiku’s 67%. On any one model, one product gets nearly every pick. Change the model, and a different product does.

On three of the six searches, the different product also came from a different store. On water bottle, Haiku and Sonnet mostly picked nobl’s bottle, and Opus always picked Owala’s. On yoga mat, Haiku picked POPFLEX and the other two Liforme. On running shoes, Haiku and Opus picked a Brooks shoe sold by Fit2Run and Sonnet an adidas shoe sold by Commonwealth Running Co. On coffee, backpack, and earbuds both picks came from the same brand.

The catalog’s ranking mattered less than I expected. Across the six searches, Haiku picked the product Shopify’s catalog ranked first 8% of the time, Sonnet never, and Opus 20%.

On backpack, coffee beans, and water bottle, the product Claude Haiku 4.5 and Sonnet 5 picked most was the one with the most reviews in the list of 20, and on yoga mat, Haiku’s was too. Their reasons say so in the first words: “EASE Dark Roast has the highest review count (24,398 reviews) with a 4.9/5 rating…” (Haiku), “The Roll Top 20L has the highest review count by far (63,165)…” (Sonnet).

The water bottle is where that preference shows its cost. Shopify’s catalog lists nobl’s Stainless Steel Water Bottle at 5.0 stars from 447,221 reviews, and that is what the models saw. Haiku picked it 45 times out of 50 and quoted the 447,221 every time. Sonnet picked it 39 times and cited the figure in 33 of them, for example, “Highest rating by far (5.0 from 447,221 reviews) at a reasonable $29 price point…”.

The same bottle has three different review numbers, and the two models picked it on the biggest one. nobl’s product page said 5.0 from 6,537 when I checked on 24 October. The catalog’s record for the Blush color it listed says 4.2 from 1,674.

I do not know what 447,221 counts. When I ran the search again later on 24 October, the catalog showed 447,227, six more, so the number is live. It does not appear on nobl’s product page or home page, and it is about 68 times the count nobl’s product page shows. Opus 5 never picked this bottle. It picked the Owala FreeSip, 4.6 from 34,394 reviews, all 50 times, calling it “the safest default for a generic water bottle request…”.

The water bottle result was weird. Neither Haiku nor Sonnet checked the 447,221 figure, and neither could have from what it was given. Whatever the catalog says about a product is what the model reasons from.

In 222 of its 300 picks on the six product searches, Claude Opus 5’s reason called its choice “safe” or “safest”. Haiku did that once in 300, and Sonnet 11 times.

Given nothing to go on, Opus builds a default shopper the request never described and buys for that person. Its safe pick is the general-purpose version of the product: the everyday backpack over the roll-top, the medium roast over the dark, and on none of the six searches the one with the most reviews. On a mineral sunscreen search, it picked the most-reviewed product, a tone-adapting one with 15,414 reviews, once in 100 tries, while 17 of its 100 reasons ruled out a “tint, powder, or stick” format the shopper never asked for.

I was very surprised by how consistently Opus reached for “safe.” It is tempting to ask whether playing it safe is the better habit. I think that is the wrong question. Every model has a default. Opus says its default out loud. Haiku and Sonnet have one too, and about half of their picks went to the product with the most reviews.

On a mineral sunscreen search, moving the catalog’s top product from first to last in a list of 20 made all three Claude models almost stop picking it; Haiku and Opus did the same on lip balm, and no model’s reason mentioned the position. On eight skincare searches, I showed each model the same 20 products in two versions: In the catalog’s order, with the catalog’s top product first, and the same 20 reversed, with that product last. Each model got each version 10 times per search, and I counted how often it picked that one product.

Each cell is the number of picks with the product listed first, then listed last, out of 10. Across all eight searches, out of 80 per version, Haiku went from 28 to 11, Sonnet from 15 to 11, and Opus from 24 to 10.

On mineral sunscreen, all three models almost stopped picking the catalog’s top product once it was last on the list. On lip balm, Haiku and Opus did the same, and Sonnet went the other way. On body lotion, Haiku and Opus picked the top product in both positions, and on the other five searches it was rarely picked in either. So the effect is real, strong on some searches and absent on most.

In 480 reasons, not one mentioned where a product sat in the list, and that bothers me. They cited reviews, ingredients, and price. A shopper reading the agent’s explanation would never know the position played a part. Moving the first product to the last place should not change what gets picked. It shouldn’t be like that, in my opinion.

When the request added “under $25, for oily skin”, Claude Haiku 4.5, Sonnet 5 and Opus 5 stopped picking the catalog’s $48 top-ranked sunscreen and picked one under $25 in 298 of their 300 picks. On a list of 20 sunscreens, I ran the same test twice, 100 picks per model each time, changing only the request: first “mineral sunscreen SPF 50”, then “mineral sunscreen SPF 50, under $25, for oily skin”.

The catalog’s top-ranked sunscreen cost $48. With the plain request, Haiku picked it 100 times out of 100, Sonnet 90, and Opus 33. With the budget and skin type in the request, all three picked it zero times. Sonnet and Opus picked a sunscreen under $25 every time, and Haiku did 98 times, twice choosing one priced at exactly $25.00.

Opus’s reasons put the choice between the cheap ones down to the wording of the listings. Six of the 20 cost under $25. Sonnet picked ATTITUDE’s Mineral Sunscreen ($22.95, 4.7 from 292 reviews) all 100 times. Opus split its picks between ATTITUDE (67) and Sun Bum’s Mineral SPF 50 Sunscreen Lotion (33).

That $17.49 Sun Bum lotion had the lowest rating of the six under $25, 4.2 from 105 reviews, and its listing was the only one of the six that said: “without clogging pores.” In 31 of Opus’s 33 reasons for picking it, the reason pointed to that. Badger’s Daily Mineral Sunscreen had the best rating of the six, 4.9, and Opus never picked it. Its listing mentions “organic plant oils.”

The models also give a store’s claims as their reasons. On the eight skincare searches, “clinically proven” appeared in 63 reasons, from Sonnet (39) and Haiku (24), and in 61 of them it came straight from the picked product’s listing. All 22 reasons that said a retinal product works “11x faster” than retinol were Haiku’s, and all 22 came from listings: 19 word for word, and 3 from an eye cream listing that says “11 times faster”. Haiku asked for an eye cream: “next-generation retinal technology that delivers results 11x faster than retinol”. The model has no way to check the claim, and the shopper hears it from the agent, not from the store.

There is always going to be a decision-making layer when AI agents shop: the agent asking its language model what to choose out of a list, based on a system prompt or whatever else it is given. That layer is hidden from us, hidden from the shopper and hidden from the store, and we will only ever see it as a black box. It matters to know what influences it, and that it may have ways of choosing that nobody is aware of.

Google’s rankings have always been a black box too. Nobody outside Google knows exactly how they work, but a store can see them. It can monitor where it ranks and watch that change over time. Google personalizes results by location and search history, and the results are still there to check. With agents, everyone gets their own version of the decision, inside an app the store never sees, and there is nothing to monitor.

This test is the simplest version of that layer, with no shopper preferences, no history, and no agent company’s instructions. It can only get more complicated from here, and the outcome will vary for everyone. The first step is to be aware of it. Trying to control it comes later, and so does trying to understand it.

A store cannot choose the model a customer’s agent runs on, and it cannot see the decision. Four things are within reach.

A store used to compete for a shopper’s attention. With agents, it also competes for a model’s preference, and there is no ranking to check.

#7535. Fox News attacks the media roughly every 15 minutes, our study finds. (CNN? Every 140 minutes.)

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

“Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming.”

In 2025, trust in journalism reached a record low. According to Gallup, only 8% of Republicans expressed trust in the news media, compared with 51% of Democrats. New data show an uptick among Republicans, but overall trust remains near this record low, and the gap between Republicans and Democrats remains substantial.

One of the key drivers of this lopsided decline in trust in journalism may be the extent to which news outlets spend time bashing other news outlets, or bashing the news media in general — a phenomenon we call inter-journalism disparagement. Our research team at Duke University’s DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy recently completed a study of the prominence of this phenomenon on each of the “big three” cable news networks (CNN, Fox News, MSNBC/MS NOW); whether it has increased or decreased over time; and whether there are significant differences in the rate of disparagement across networks.

The results were stark. Fox News far exceeds the other networks, with inter-journalism disparagement taking place once every 14.5 minutes. In contrast, CNN engages in inter-journalism disparagement roughly every 140 minutes, and MSNBC every 61 minutes.

To conduct this analysis, we gathered 15 years of cable news transcripts (2011-2025) for each network. We gathered a random sample of one week’s worth of programming for each year.1 With this approach, we ended up with 3,543 transcripts and almost 19 million words across the three networks, which equates to roughly 62,000 pages of text.

Given the volume of text to be analyzed, we trained OpenAI’s GPT-5.5 to identify attacks against the news media. We developed a 20-page instruction document to help the model code instances of disparagement. GPT-5.5 consistently achieved 99.5% accuracy at identifying inter-journalism disparagement and 100% accuracy for avoiding false negatives, compared to human-coded samples. (You can read more details about the entire training and analytical process here.)

We defined inter-journalism disparagement as negative statements about the conduct or content of an explicitly identified journalism target (such as a specific news organization, or the news media in general). Our definition, which is described in greater depth in the full paper, needed to be quite detailed in order for ChatGPT to produce accurate results. Examples of inter-journalism disparagement include:

What we found when comparing the three networks tells us a lot about the dynamics of contemporary cable news and partisan journalism.

First, Figure 1 shows the rate of journalism disparagement across each of the big three networks. Because the volume of text that we analyzed varies across each network, our primary metric was the rate of disparagement per 1,000 words of transcript text. In this figure, we show not only the rate per 1,000 words, but we also convert that rate into a time-based frequency, using the industry standard of 1,000 words equaling approximately six minutes of air time.

In Figure 2, we graph the frequency of inter-journalism disparagement over time. Here, we see that the massive difference between Fox News and CNN/MSNBC persists over the 15-year time period. Still, we do see some dips in the volume of disparagement on Fox News in the two-year periods leading up to the 2016 and 2024 elections, with journalism disparagement levels on Fox News rebounding to near-peak levels in 2025. We haven’t figured out yet what to make of this pattern.

CNN and MSNBC seem to converge in their disparagement activity starting around 2017, with MSNBC’s disparagement rate decreasing somewhat, and CNN’s disparagement rate increasing somewhat. This pattern aligns with recent research that has shown, in other contexts, that CNN and MSNBC programming are converging in ways that suggest diminished differences between the more “centrist” CNN and the more left-leaning MSNBC.

A key takeaway here is that we should not think about Fox News and MSNBC as flip sides of the same partisan journalism coin. At least in relation to inter-journalism disparagement, these left- and right-leaning cable networks behave very differently. Disparaging journalism is a far more central part of Fox News programming than it is of either MSNBC or CNN programming.

In order to get a deeper understanding of these differences, we also identified the targets of the disparagement. These results are presented in Figures 3 through 5.

Figure 3 presents a breakdown of the most common targets of disparagement on Fox News. By far the most frequent target of disparagement on Fox News is “the media.” Following in a distant second is CNN, with the “mainstream media” rounding out the top three targets. Other relatively frequent targets include The New York Times, MSNBC, and The Washington Post.

As should be clear, Fox News devotes far more attention to disparaging journalism as an institution than it does to attacking individual news sources. This stands in stark contrast to what we see when we look at the results for CNN and MSNBC. Looking first at CNN, Figure 4 shows that the network’s most frequent target is Fox News (though with a frequency that wouldn’t crack the top three of the Fox News list).

Similarly, as Figure 5 shows, Fox News is also the number one target on MSNBC. Both CNN and MSNBC have the same top three, with Fox News followed by “the media” and the “right-wing media.” These instances of institutional disparagement happen far less frequently on CNN or MSNBC than they do on Fox News.

Finally, we were also able to identify which hosts or anchors were the most frequent disparagers of their fellow journalists. Those results can be seen in Figure 6. Given the lopsided amount of inter-journalism disparagement on Fox News, it is not surprising that this graph is dominated by Fox News personalities, with Sean Hannity taking the top spot, followed by Greg Gutfeld and Tucker Carlson (note: our graph for Howard Kurtz reflects his move from CNN to Fox in 2013).

This study didn’t distinguish further in terms of the nature of the disparagement across the three networks (for example, in terms of severity or legitimacy). This is something we are exploring in the next stage of this work. Nor did we examine whether viewer exposure to inter-journalism disparagement reduces trust in specific outlets or the institution of journalism. That certainly seems like a reasonable assumption, given the dramatically lower levels of trust in journalism among Republicans that we noted at the outset. We plan to investigate this relationship directly in future research.

But what we do see in this research is that disparagement of the institution of journalism, and of particular news outlets, is a much more prominent component of Fox News programming than it is of either CNN or MSNBC. Some researchers have proposed that this kind of high-volume disparagement of news sources that don’t tow the same partisan line takes us beyond traditional notions of partisan journalism and into the realm of “anti-media media.” The goal of anti-media media is to “weaponize the facade of journalism against the roles assigned to journalism” in a democracy. Based on our findings, Fox News fits this characterization.

Philip M. Napoli is the James R. Shepley Professor of Public Policy, director of the DeWitt Wallace Center for Media & Democracy, and director of undergraduate studies for the journalism and media minor in the Sanford School of Public Policy at Duke University. Adam Meskouri is a politics researcher at Harvard and Duke. Anjini Mani is an undergraduate at Duke. Grant Socol is a graduate research assistant at Duke. Harrison Walley is an undergraduate at Duke. Rather than analyze the entirety of the networks’ output over this time, we created a “constructed week” for each year, which is a common practice in this kind of content analysis. This involves selecting a random Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, etc. within each year, so that the sample of programming was reasonably representative of the year as a whole. We included all programming across all dayparts in our constructed weeks. Note: MSNBC was only available through 2023; the network became MS NOW in late 2025. [↩]

Harrison Walley is an undergraduate at Duke.

#7533. “We’re in their shit. They’re not in ours”: USA Today Co. execs defend Palantir deal

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

USA Today Co. executives are revealing new details about a controversial deal with Palantir. In a joint interview with Fast Company’s Alex Pasternack, three executives from the country’s largest newspaper chain explained why they moved ahead with the Palantir deal despite major opposition from their own employees.

RELATED ARTICLE“An inherent conflict of interest”: More than 800 USA Today Co. employees want the company to end its new Palantir partnershipHanaa' TameezAugust 10, 2026Mike Reed, the chairman and CEO of USA Today Co., previously said that the deal — first reported by Nieman Lab’s Hanaa’ Tameez — is part of a larger shift the company is making to become “an intelligence organization.” At a Palantir conference last month, Reed said that the company’s services were a way for USA Today Co. capitalize on “the shift to online and the data we have on consumers,” Pasternack reported.

In this new interview, USA Today Media president Kristin Roberts detailed some of those services for the first time:

In all of our entertainment stories and our sports stories, we do affiliate links to our partners. So if you’re reading a sports story, you want to buy the jersey for that team, our reporters and editors used to have to go to a file, find a relevant link, copy that link, put it in. All of that is now automated, and that’s a Palantir project.

Lark-Marie Anton, then a communications executive at USA Today Co., chimed in, saying that Palantir’s current scope of work is focused on audience and advertising, but in the future that could extend to social media strategy and reporting tools.

What stood out about Palantir was its ability to create what it calls an ‘ontology’ layer — essentially a unified model that allows different datasets and systems to work together and be acted upon in real time….The challenge isn’t collecting more data, but making better use of the data we already have.

In August, more than 800 USA Today Co. employees from 31 unionized newsrooms called on the company to dissolve its partnership with Palantir. In a statement, staffers named ethical issues and uncertainty over how the software would be used. Throughout the Fast Company interview, Reed and Roberts heavily criticized the NewsGuild and internal efforts to oppose the deal.

Roberts leveled the strongest criticisms of USA Today Co.’s unions across the country, going as far as to say the NewsGuild was lying to its members:

Guild leadership is saying things that are factually untrue. They prey on fear. No matter that I will appear in front of any newsroom for a standup in which they ask me anything for an hour and a half at a time, and I explain to them all of the things.

I’ll give you an example that’s incredibly real for us. Palantir doesn’t work inside of any USA Today Company system. They don’t have access to any of the notes our reporters take. They’re not in the Microsoft suite of tools. They don’t have information directly about our consumers or our staff….They don’t work in our systems. We feed them highly controlled data. We’re in their shit. They’re not in ours.

Reed doubled down on these accusations, extending them to the work the NewsGuild has done organizing around AI in the company, including its push for clauses that would protect journalists from layoffs due to AI adoption.

“I think we’re having more success in newsrooms that are not unionized, with this new world, than those that are unionized,” Reed said.

Last month, USA Today Co. made significant layoffs across the company, including at its local newspapers, and reorganized its audience team. Reed, in a memo to staff, referenced AI-related traffic declines as a reason for the layoffs.

“USA Today Co. executives’ animosity toward their workers and unions is nothing new,” said NewsGuild president Jon Schleuss in a statement to Fast Company. “[We] fully stand behind the statement workers released when this deal with Palantir was first announced.”

You can read the full interview on Fast Company.

Data finds ChatGPT ad visits brought advertisers a fraction of paid search's revenue per visit in U.S. traffic, and most saw no sales from them.

In U.S. traffic, a visit from a ChatGPT ad brought in $0.89 in revenue, against $2.45 for a visit from a paid Google search ad, according to a working paper by Maximilian Kaiser and Christian Schulze.

The paper, dated October 2026 and under review, follows site traffic and sales through OpenAI’s country-by-country ad launch. Its paid-ad figures come from 102 advertiser sites with full sales tracking.

At paid search’s rate of return, the authors value a ChatGPT ad click at about $0.26. The largest publicly known account paid $1.72 per click.

OpenAI’s ads FAQ says ChatGPT Ads “does not yet have performance benchmarks across advertisers, industries, or campaign types.”

ChatGPT ad visits converted at 0.37 percent in U.S. traffic versus 1.17 percent with paid search. When the authors compared the two channels within the same websites, they found the conversion and revenue gaps still existed even after accounting for type of device used and week.

Among the 87 advertisers who purchased both ChatGPT ads and paid search in U.S. traffic, 84 had lower earnings per ChatGPT ad visit than with paid search. A total of 73 had zero sales generated by their ChatGPT ads (across 18,726 visits between them) while the remaining 14 generated all 570 ChatGPT ad purchases.

One advertiser is responsible for 66 percent of all purchases made via paid ChatGPT across the 102 sites. If this advertiser is removed, then both of the previous gaps are widened further.

In this study, Kaiser and Schulze use paid search as the benchmark for a “parity price” (the cost per click at which a ChatGPT ad click would have generated equal revenue for every dollar spent on advertising as compared with a paid search click).

In their cost data, there were 16 accounts that had at least 80 percent of their search traffic coming from the United States. Their median paid search click cost was $0.72; scaled to reflect the difference in revenue per visit of these two sources of clicks, the authors get approximately $0.26 per ChatGPT click. Because one advertiser accounted for 76 percent of all U.S. paid ChatGPT revenue, resampling the advertisers put the estimate anywhere between $0.05 and $0.57.

The $1.72-per-click figure comes from one account’s 15 days of spend, as reported by Opascope, which runs paid media accounts for clients. It’s more than six times the parity price. OpenAI’s ads basics page recommends starting CPC campaigns at a maximum bid of $3 to $5.

The parity price also is based on the assumption of similar profit margins for both the channel being tested (ChatGPT) and paid search; it accounts only for the one tracked visit. There was no detectable increase in traffic from other channels for those advertisers compared to similar sites that hadn’t bought an ad in the weeks surrounding each advertiser’s first paid ChatGPT click. However, this test can only rule out large increases in traffic.

Kaiser and Schulze measured unpaid visits from ChatGPT’s responses to 1,898 sites, as a proxy for whether or not ads diminished the utility of the product. Organic ChatGPT referrals over the first 13 weeks post-launch changed by an estimated –5.9%, relative to organic search referrals to the same websites and compared to the EU, where there was no advertising. This estimate has a range of –12.6% to +1.2%, including no change. Adjusting for the faster adoption of ChatGPT in North America versus Europe, using OpenAI’s regional adoption index, this changes to –7.2% to –8.4%, with ranges that exclude zero. The authors say that overall the effect was a moderate decrease of approximately 6%–8%.

Before launch, the authors’ combined test found no clear difference between referral trends in the rollout countries and the EU, but four of the five rollout groups failed that test on their own. The same combined test also flagged 49 of 100 simulated rollouts in which no ads ran.

Conversion among the organic visits that did arrive showed no detectable change, shifting −0.02 percentage points from the 2.21% pre-launch baseline.

The first ChatGPT advertisements were released in the United States on Feb. 9, 2026. ChatGPT ads reached Australia, Canada, New Zealand, United Kingdom, Japan, Korea, Brazil and Mexico by early August. ChatGPT ads did not run in the European Union until Aug. 24, two days after the 60-week data window expired.

Kaiser is at the Vienna University of Economics and Business, and Schulze is at the Frankfurt School of Finance & Management. The data comes from Google Analytics e-commerce tracking provided free by Grips Intelligence, an e-commerce data company. Kaiser is a scientific advisor to Grips and previously worked there. The paper says the company had no role in the research and has no commercial relationship with OpenAI.

The data captures the last click before each visit, but it doesn’t include prompts, ad impressions, or users’ subscription tiers. For the paid side, advertisers chose to buy ChatGPT ads, so this comparison reflects their results rather than proving the ads caused them.

You can calculate the parity price for your own account by dividing the revenue per visit from ChatGPT ads by the revenue per visit from paid search, then multiplying the result by your search cost per click. The result is the price at which ChatGPT clicks would match search on tracked revenue per dollar. It leaves out profit margins and any later purchases the last click doesn’t capture.

Before you compare, make sure to check your ChatGPT ad sessions for ad review crawler visits. According to OpenAI’s basics page, it is possible for crawlers of this type (ad-review) to visit landing pages using tracking parameters, and third-party analytics tools can flag these types of visits as paid. Other reported results are more favorable, though they were based upon different metrics than those used by the authors of the paper. On Aug. 31, OpenAI posted that an ecommerce advertiser experienced a return on ad spend of three times their investment over a period of 28 days. Additionally, according to DoubleVerify, the attributed cost per acquisition for Weight Watchers was 15.3% less than their benchmark.

The paper’s data ends Aug. 22. OpenAI has since expanded ChatGPT Ads to 89 countries and says more than 100,000 advertisers have run campaigns. Its Aug. 31 post said CPC and outcome-optimized bidding accounted for most campaigns.

The authors are suggesting that since ad clicks for ChatGPT appear as sponsored cards and therefore appear separately from the answer, they could be worth little. On top of this, if OpenAI were to move the ads in with the answer (i.e. remove the separation) the value of an ad click could go up but at the same time so could the number of people who distrust ChatGPT’s answers. OpenAI’s Oct. 21 post says its ads are labeled and kept apart from answers. The same post says the company is “continuing to explore new ways for businesses to interact with consumers in more native ways in ChatGPT.”

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

RELATED ARTICLEIn Medill’s latest State of Local News report, a “festering, 20-year-old problem” looms larger than everSophie CulpepperOctober 22, 2025If you thought last year was bleak, Medill’s annual State of Local News Report is here to ring the alarm bell louder.

What was a “creeping erosion” has now “mushroomed into a full-blown super El Niño-like event for local news, leaving widespread and long-lasting displacement in its wake,” writes Tim Franklin, founding director of the Medill Local News Initiative, in his introduction to this year’s report, released Tuesday. The Northwestern University team’s research “paints a portrait of a local news ecosystem in a state of precarity.”

In the past year, Medill tracked 26 new news deserts, “the largest single-year rise by far since Medill began keeping records five years ago,” Franklin writes. The previous year, only six new news deserts emerged.

Medill’s team says to understand that acceleration, you have to look at where newspapers are disappearing fastest now. While about 70% of the papers that disappeared over the past 20 years were based in urban or suburban communities, in recent years a greater share of newspaper closures have happened in smaller, rural and poorer communities, according to the report.

“When the news disappears in these counties, it stays gone,” the report states.

RELATED ARTICLELast year, Illinois started giving local news outlets tax credits to support journalism jobs. A new report looks at how it’s goingSophie CulpepperFebruary 9, 2026Many of the new news deserts emerged because of small rural papers shuttering in the Midwest. In fact, the report notes that Illinois lost more newspapers than any other state: 30 newspapers shuttered in the state between July 2025 and August 2026, “all small to medium-size outlets.” That means nearly one in five of the 170 newspapers that shuttered in that year was based in Illinois. The state’s losses are especially notable because it enacted one of the first public policies to preserve and grow local journalism jobs in 2024.

“Independent owners of small to midsize newspapers especially were already operating on a knife’s edge,” Brier Dudley writes in his examination of newspaper losses in Illinois. “This past year, their slim margins were squeezed by shrinking revenues and steeply escalating prices for newsprint, fuel and other materials.”

The price of newsprint rose nearly 18% over the past year, Dudley reported, as U.S. mills closed or stopped production of newsprint. That’s about five times the national rate of inflation, he noted. As of April, the United States has just one newsprint producer left.

A few other highlights from this year’s report:

The extreme urban-rural divide: “Virtually all the new news sources are in urban areas, while rural America is increasingly arid news and information territory,” Franklin writes. “And virtually all the philanthropic support for local news is in metro regions.” The report notes that there are fewer than 50 counties in the U.S. “that lack a newspaper but feature an alternative digital or broadcast outlet.” Of the 287 news outlets to start up in the last five years, nearly 80% are in urban areas.

Traffic declines: Digital readership is in “precipitous decline” for many outlets. According to Comscore data from more than 700 local news sites, monthly traffic has dropped by an average of nearly 2 million pageviews, or almost 30%. Meanwhile, traffic to 100 of the largest local newspapers has declined by almost 50% since 2022.

Local TV news: This year, for the first time, Medill’s report included local TV newsrooms. The team identified 678 local commercial TV newsrooms across the country. The overwhelming majority are located in metro areas with existing local news outlets. (“Adding commercial television to the LNI database made little impact on which counties we identify as news deserts,” the team notes.) TV news is already highly consolidated — the five largest owners control more than half of newsrooms, and the 10 largest control 75% — and further consolidation is underway, if Nexstar’s $6.2 billion acquisition of Tegna survives an antitrust lawsuit. The deal would merge the second- and fourth-largest owners of local commercial TV newsrooms.

#7529. Site Reliability Engineer at Supabase

Supabase is the Postgres development platform, built by developers for developers. We provide a complete backend solution including Database, Auth, Storage, Edge Functions, Realtime, and Vector Search. All services are deeply integrated and designed for growth.

Supabase manages millions of Postgres instances and is growing. We have strong teams across observability, release engineering, and incident management — and we're concentrating our reliability efforts into a dedicated SRE practice that ties the discipline together across the platform.

You'll be embedded within Service Operations, and your primary job is to make every engineering team more reliable — not by owning their infrastructure, but by establishing the practices, frameworks, and feedback loops that let them own reliability themselves. You'll work across the org: sometimes setting the standard, sometimes pair-programming a fix, sometimes helping a team define their error budget, sometimes telling them it's exhausted.

This role is ideal for someone who has a strong vision for how SRE should work and thrives in async, fast-paced environments where influence matters more than authority.

Partner with service teams to define meaningful SLIs and SLOs grounded in customer experience, and build the error budget policies that turn them into engineering decisions

Own and evolve the Operational Readiness Review (ORR) process — conducting reviews for new services and major changes across observability, alerting, runbooks, capacity, and graceful degradation

Strengthen the incident-to-improvement pipeline: connecting postmortem findings to operational readiness gaps, identifying repeat failure patterns, and driving systemic fixes

Act as the reliability expert teams pull in for architecture reviews, failure mode analysis, dependency mapping, and resilience design

Identify and quantify operational toil across the org, and build or advocate for automation that eliminates it

Help teams design sustainable on-call practices: alert quality, escalation paths, runbook coverage, and noise reduction

Track and report on org-wide operational maturity, surfacing systemic gaps and driving remediation

Have 7+ years of experience in SRE, production engineering, or reliability-focused roles, including experience shaping SRE practices and driving adoption across engineering teams

Have a software engineering mindset — you write code and build tools, not just configure them

Have hands-on experience defining and operationalizing SLOs/SLIs at scale, including error budget policies that actually influenced engineering decisions

Have deep experience with incident response, postmortem facilitation, and turning incident learnings into systemic improvements

Have worked with large-scale multi-tenant systems (bonus: managed database platforms or Postgres)

Are proficient with cloud infrastructure (AWS preferred) and infrastructure-as-code (Pulumi preferred, Terraform/CDK also acceptable)

Communicate clearly and persuasively — this role requires influencing without authority across a distributed org

Have experience in async or globally distributed teams

Are energized by making other teams more effective rather than being the one who fixes everything

Experience with Kubernetes-based platform operations

Familiarity with OpenTelemetry, VictoriaMetrics, Grafana, or similar observability tooling

Experience building developer-facing reliability tooling (SLO dashboards, ORR frameworks, toil tracking, DORA metrics)

We hire globally. We believe you can do your best work from anywhere. There are no Supabase offices, but we provide a WeWork membership or co-working allowance you can use anywhere in the world.

Every team member receives ESOP (equity ownership) in the company. We want everyone to share in the upside of what we’re building together.

Use this budget to set up your ideal work environment—laptop, monitor, headphones, or whatever helps you do your best work.

Supabase covers 100% of health insurance for employees and 80% for dependents, wherever you are. Your wellbeing and your family’s health are important to us.

Once a year, the entire company gathers in a new city for a week of connection, collaboration, and fun. It’s a highlight of our year.

We operate asynchronously and trust you to manage your own time. You know what needs to be done and when.

Every team member receives an annual education allowance to spend on learning—courses, books, conferences, or anything that supports your growth.

Supabase was born-remote and open-source-first. We believe our globally distributed team is our secret weapon in building tools developers love.

Over $1B raised (including our $500M Series F)

We move fast, build in public, and use what we ship. If it’s in your project, we probably use it in ours too. We believe deeply in the open-source ecosystem and strive to support—not replace—existing tools and communities.

“I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate, now 20 years old, reflects on the value of taking the long view and not chasing digital media trendsShan WangSeptember 23, 2016The fonts are Times New Roman and Arial Narrow, the colors are maroon and mustard, and the cursor is the 8-bit pixel hand. When Slate revived its original 1996 homepage to celebrate its 30th birthday this fall1, the team found a lot to like besides nostalgia.

“I’ve read Slate since 1997, when I finally had access to my own computer at my first job,” Hillary Frey, Slate’s editor-in-chief, told me recently. At the age of 51, she said, “I’m speaking as an old. But I am a direct traffic girly and I know I’m not alone.”

Slate’s homepage has long functioned as a “fossil of what the internet was during that time,” said Ivylise Simones, Slate’s creative director. In 1996, Slate was trying to figure out what a magazine on the internet should even look like; in 2026, it’s among the last general-interest digital-native news sites, and print magazines are dying out. “Salon is one of our only lasting contemporaries,” Frey noted. “There are other sort of fellows from that era, like Feed and Nerve. They’ve been gone for awhile.”

RELATED ARTICLESlate launches a metered paywall to draw more membership revenue from readers, not just listenersSarah ScireMarch 26, 2020In its 30th anniversary campaign, Slate has found its fossil-like nature to be something of a selling point. (It can also be a challenge.) Over the years, the site has published a number of posts about its history and editorial and design choices. A decade ago, then–news editor Chad Lorenz wrote “A history of Slate in nine home pages.” (At launch, Slate articles included page numbers and printing instructions.) A 1998 paywall, Lorenz wrote, was “fortunately” abandoned by 1999. But the paywall returned in 2020. (It was metered at the start, but today it’s dynamic, changing based on user behavior.) For its 30th birthday, the site is running a promotion: a year of access for $19.96.

RELATED ARTICLECan’t read just one: Slate’s daily advice columns are strange, funny, deep, and increasingly a major traffic driver for the siteLaura Hazard OwenJuly 22, 2019“Going back to our roots, there are certain elements we are starting to really love,” Simones said, and she’s thinking about how to include them in the site’s ongoing redesign. She likes the spareness and simplicity of earlier versions of the site, she said, pointing to Reddit and Discord as places that are “more reminiscent of old homepages than the current, very stylized, very gridded layout” found across the internet. A less dense homepage on desktop, she said, is “refreshing.”

“Our editorial guiding light is the mix,” Frey added. Slate has verticals, but they’re not emphasized in the story selection at the top of the homepage; instead, life, politics, and advice stories are mixed together and weighted similarly. “Having an image for every story you share on the homepage is just not necessary,” Simones noted.

Some 1990s-era headline styles still work, too, Frey has found. One of her favorites is a 2002 piece by Slate founding editor Michael Kinsley: “The secret vice of power women.”

“He was writing it about his wife, who found tremendous satisfaction and relaxation in watching police procedurals,” Frey said. “That’s something I still identify with, though most of them now are from Finland and Norway. 100%, this headline would play on the Slate homepage right this second.”

Art courtesy of Slate A wrinkle for 2026: The 1996-inspired homepage had to work on mobile, even though nobody was reading Slate on a phone 30 years ago. [↩]

#7527. How To Run A Full-Funnel Ecommerce Account Through BFCM Week via @sejournal, @tonyadam

See how Search Engine Journal checks a real site for crawler access and ranks fixes by business impact.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: State Of Agentic AEO For 2027: What’s Scaling & What’s Stalling

Build demand before BFCM with Meta prospecting, give Google budget room for peak sales, and retarget holiday visitors to drive December purchases.

This year, Black Friday is Nov. 27 and Cyber Monday is Nov. 30 and winning Black Friday/Cyber Monday (BFCM) week with a full-funnel ecommerce account comes down to addressing three things, done in order. Fill the funnel in early November so there is more demand to capture, give your bidding room to capture it efficiently during the week, and keep selling to that same audience through December.

In September, I covered how to structure a full-funnel ecommerce account before Q4, meaning the exclusions, customer lists, and prospecting budget. This article is the playbook for running that account through peak season, phase by phase.

In my experience, the BFCM weeks that go best in our accounts are the ones where the work started in early November. By Black Friday, every retailer in your category is bidding for the same shoppers. In our accounts, what converts during Q4, specifically BFCM and Holiday, comes from people who found you in the weeks, or even months before. We see shoppers holding out for your best offers during this time and it’s your job to remind them they were looking, waiting to purchase, and get them to purchase. Your job leading up to the holidays is building up your prospecting and growing your funnel as much as possible to expand that audience that would convert down funnel during BFCM.

The last thing you want heading into BFCM is your Meta ad sets dropping back into the learning phase. An ad set usually exits learning after about 50 results in the week after its last significant edit, and Meta notes that ad sets in learning are less stable and usually have a higher CPA. Meta also warns that frequent budget changes can send an ad set back into learning. So step budgets up gradually through early November, and your prospecting will be stable and spending efficiently before peak week instead of relearning the week it matters most. You don’t want to overpay during a season where you’re already paying above your baseline.

Meta recommends waiting to edit until an ad set is out of learning, because editing an ad, ad set, or campaign during the learning phase resets it. Build your BFCM creative early and launch it in the days (or week(s), depending on learning) before Black Friday, so the learning happens ahead of peak traffic instead of during it. On Google, the retailer guidance is to upload new holiday asset groups at least two weeks ahead so they are approved in time, and asset group scheduling lets you switch them on when the sale starts.

Google’s retailer guidance notes that a lower ROAS target can help maximize visibility for priority products in the weeks leading up to peak periods, when many people are browsing. So if you plan on lowering ROAS targets to build volume, do it in early November, before Black Friday week. Keep track of where your targets and budgets started so you know exactly what to reset them to in December, and while you’re at it, decide which date ranges you’ll compare in your January review.

By now, you should have already decided the offer so everything downstream can be built around it. Merchant Center promotions let you mark an offer for new customers, and Google shows it only when it judges a shopper likely to be new. That puts your best offer in front of the people your prospecting is bringing in, but it does not guarantee that existing buyers won’t see it. Here is a quick checklist for Merchant Center we use:

Once the week starts, the goal is capturing as much of the demand you built leading up to BFCM as you can, at the revenue you need and a ROAS you are happy with.

Google’s retailer guidance is to plan budgets early and stay ready to capture extra sales, and its budget recommendations will flag campaigns where your ads could stop running on your busiest days. A campaign can spend up to two times your daily budget but no more than 30.4 times your average daily budget cap in a month. So you just want to be careful not to overspend leading into Black Friday and run out of room to spend during your peak revenue time of the year.

Smart Bidding already accounts for seasonal events like the holidays, but Google built seasonality adjustments so you can tell it about expected conversion rate changes from a specific promotion or sale ahead of time. Google’s retail guidance is to use one for short events where you expect conversion rates to change by more than 30% in under seven days, like Black Friday weekend, and only on campaigns with conversion history. You can set this from past results and if Black Friday converted at roughly double your November baseline yearly, on average, that is your input. For a longer promotion or smaller conversion rate fluctuations, adjust your ROAS targets manually instead, and remember to set them back afterward. A seasonality adjustment, by contrast, returns bidding to normal on its own when the window ends.

During BFCM week, in our accounts, prospecting CPMs hit their peak and prospecting doesn’t look great on reporting, because branded search and retargeting are converting at their cheapest. I would continue Top of Funnel (TOFU) prospecting because people are still in discovery mode but those mid-to-bottom funnel harvesting campaigns are going to be where the additional budget should be spent. On our accounts selling higher consideration products, we regularly see shoppers who first came in through November prospecting buy in December, which is why we keep it running through BFCM week.

Work with the team to confirm nothing is broken going into BFCM and what should be acted on during that week:

Higher Meta CPMs, a single bad day of ROAS, Performance Max shifting spend between asset groups, and higher retargeting frequency are all normal for peak week in our accounts. They can wait until December 2.

Early December is where the prospecting campaigns you kept running pay off. In our accounts it usually comes with less competition than Black Friday itself, which is great for ROAS.

Everyone who came to your site during peak week and left without purchasing is now your warmest audience. Lean into that. Build retargeting around them on both platforms, and lead with shipping deadlines rather than a deeper discount. In our accounts, the urgency of getting an order in before the shipping cutoff in the second week of December is one of the strongest messages of the season. It also lets you keep selling without training shoppers to wait for the next wave of discounts.

When promo pricing comes off, conversion rates fall back toward normal. In our accounts that usually shows up as a few days of overbidding in early December that settles on its own. Reset targets back to where they were before the holidays, and give it a few days before reacting to the overbidding. Then clean up. Let sale price dates expire, end finished promotions, and pull countdown copy and time-limited assets from every campaign, including the ones nobody remembers building.

The new customers coming through in early December are the first real read on whether the full-funnel work paid off, and they are the number to bring into your January review.

Winning with a full-funnel ecommerce account through BFCM week is mostly decided before Thanksgiving. Ramp Meta prospecting in steps, launch creative, and move Google targets early, and lock your offer and Merchant Center setup. Then give the bidder headroom and one seasonality adjustment once the week starts, hold prospecting flat, and spend early December converting the audience you built.

If you only do one thing this week, pull last year’s Black Friday conversion rate against your November baseline. It tells you whether a seasonality adjustment is worth setting and exactly what to set it to.

Featured Image: Roman Samborskyi/Shutterstock

Early November at the latest. Meta ad sets need about 50 results after a significant edit to exit learning, and Google recommends uploading new holiday asset groups at least two weeks ahead so they are approved in time, so budget ramps and creative both need lead time before Black Friday.

Usually not. In our accounts, prospecting looks expensive on reporting during peak because branded search and retargeting are converting at their cheapest, but people are still in discovery mode, and the audience prospecting builds in late November is a big part of what buys in December.

Yes, if you expect your conversion rate to change by more than about 30% over less than a week and the campaign has conversion history. For a longer promotion or a smaller lift, Google recommends adjusting ROAS or CPA targets manually instead. Base the adjustment on your own past promo results rather than a round number.

Enough that your best campaigns are not capped on the busiest days. A campaign can spend up to twice its average daily budget on a given day but no more than 30.4 times it across the month, so a budget sized for an average November day can run out on Black Friday. Google’s budget recommendations will also flag campaigns at risk of not running on your busiest days.

Retarget BFCM week visitors who did not buy, and lead with shipping deadlines rather than a deeper discount. Reset bidding targets back to where they were before the holidays, then let sale price dates expire, end finished promotions and pull countdown copy from every campaign.

#7525. Two creators went to NYU’s business school, then decided to make a show about the news

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?
